## Deep read
The trap works because attention obeys the first wording it hears. Once the teen reader reads the problem as "break up or not," every fact starts serving that ballot. A sister's comment becomes evidence for leaving. A sweet text becomes evidence for staying. The relationship, the family pressure, and the timing all get flattened into one door.

Quaker's Snapple deal shows the same squeeze at corporate size. The Quaker executive studies a packet with Snapple on the cover and about $1.8 billion on the price line. The page says acquisition, but the deeper problem is growth. If the meeting treats Snapple as the growth plan, the group may argue valuation while skipping other paths.

Money makes the missing path easier to see. Opportunity cost is plain: every dollar, hour, or bit of attention used here cannot be used there. A price tag is also a mirror. It asks what else the same resources could do.

Two small tests help. First, listen for whether-or-not wording. Should we buy Snapple? Should the teen reader end it? That wording is a warning light, not a verdict. Second, make the visible options disappear for a moment. If this choice vanished, what would you try next? The test does not pick the winner. It makes the room less captive.

A bigger frame is not a bigger mess. Wider does not mean endless. It means at least one more real path before judgment begins. You cannot compare what you never allowed on the table.

## Full read
Too much widening can become a fog machine. A team can add ten weak options, praise its own creativity, and still dodge the hard work. The teen reader can list every possible text, talk, pause, and apology without ever facing the relationship pattern. Quaker could have filled a whiteboard with growth words while leaving Snapple as the only serious bet.

The useful move is narrower than brainstorming. It asks for a credible alternative that serves the same need. For the teen reader, the need may be relief from family pressure, clearer boundaries, or an honest talk about the relationship. "Break up" and "stay" are not the only handles. The problem may ask for a conversation with the partner, a boundary with family, or a slower decision after the latest fight cools.

In a company, the need may be growth. A Snapple acquisition is one possible answer. The wider frame asks what else could use about $1.8 billion. Better distribution, product repair, smaller tests, or a different deal might appear. Those paths may still lose. The gain is that the deal must beat something real.

The four frame wideners keep the work practical: Spot whether-or-not wording, Name opportunity costs, Run the Vanishing Options Test, and Ask for both-and possibilities. The exact names matter because each one catches a different squeeze. Whether-or-not wording catches the false ballot. Opportunity cost catches the hidden tradeoff. The Vanishing Options Test catches fixation. Both-and questions catch a tradeoff that may be designed around.

Both-and does not mean magic. Some choices truly conflict. A teen may not be able to protect every relationship at once. A company may not be able to buy Snapple and fund every other plan. The move is to test the tradeoff before bowing to it. A false either-or is expensive even when the stakes are small.

The corporate case also warns against status heat. A large deal can start to feel brave because it is large. A board packet, a price tag, and a public story make the option look serious. Other paths can look timid because they are less dramatic. Drama is not proof. Size can make a narrow frame louder.

Decision research is useful in the background here: many organizations have treated one real alternative as enough. That pattern should make the reader suspicious of a polished single option. A clean memo can still be cramped. A confident team can still be arguing inside a box.

The overcorrection is option tourism. People wander from idea to idea so they never have to commit. Widening the frame is not a license to delay forever. It earns a better decision by making one extra serious path visible, then comparing. The work begins before judgment, but it must end in judgment. A wider frame is a doorway, not a place to live.
